title: Back then
goal: Tell stories about the past with the imperfect, recognize the -ba- insert, and tell ongoing actions and old habits apart from single events.
bekal: form the imperfect for all four verb groups
describe childhood habits in natural sentences

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Avia narrat
dialogs.intro: Livia, Marcus and Iulia's grandmother, comes to visit. All of Grandma's stories begin with one word: olim.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: Grandma, where did you live back then?

lines.speaker: Livia:
lines.text: Olim in villa parva habitabam, prope mare.
lines.id: Back then I lived in a small house, near the sea.
lines.literal: once in house-in small-in live-I-was, near sea.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: Near the sea! Did you swim every day?

lines.speaker: Livia:
lines.id: I swam every day, and I saw fish.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Was there a school in the town?

lines.speaker: Livia:
lines.text: Erat, sed parva erat. Duodecim discipuli eramus.
lines.id: There was, but it was small. There were only twelve of us.
lines.literal: is-it-was, but small-fem is-it-was. twelve pupil-pl are-we-was.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Twelve! And was the teacher strict?

lines.speaker: Livia:
lines.text: Severissimus! Semper clamabat et tabulam pulsabat.
lines.id: Extremely strict! He was always shouting and banging the board.
lines.literal: strictest-masc! always shout-he-was and board-obj bang-he-was.

lines.speaker: Livia:
lines.text: Numquam tacebamus! Ridebamus et fabulas narrabamus.
lines.id: We were never quiet! We laughed and told stories.
lines.literal: never be-quiet-we-was! laugh-we-was and story-pl-obj tell-we-was.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: So you were just like us!

lines.speaker: Livia:
lines.text: Omnes pueri similes sunt, mi Marce. Et semper erant.
lines.id: All children are alike, my dear Marcus. And they always were.
lines.literal: all-pl boy-pl alike-pl are-they, my-call Marcus-call. and always are-they-was.

notes: **One insert for everything: -ba-.** *Habito* → *habitabam*, *video* → *videbam*, *narro* → *narrabam*, *taceo* → *tacebam*. The insert *-ba-* goes between the verb stem and the person ending, and it works in all four groups without exception. This is the easiest tense in all of Latin.

**The person endings are almost the same — except the first.** The "I" form uses *-m*, not *-o*: *habitabam*, not *habitabo*. The rest are the usual *-s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt*. Remember this well, because *habitabo* also exists — "I will live", which you learn in Unit 16.

**The imperfect describes the background, not the event.** *Habitabam* means "I used to live" or "I was living at the time" — something ongoing, repeated, or setting the scene. For an event completed once ("I moved", "he came"), Latin uses another form, which arrives in Unit 13.

**Mi Marce — an affectionate address.** *Meus* has an irregular calling form: *mi*. So *mi fili* ("my son"), *mi amice* ("my friend"), *mi Marce*. This address shows up again and again in Cicero's letters.

sections.title: The imperfect in all four groups

blocks.text: Take the verb stem, add *-ba-*, then add the person ending. Groups three and four insert an *-e-* first, so the insert becomes *-eba-*.

Mixed group three follows group four: *facio* → *faciebam*, *capio* → *capiebam*. So the whole imperfect system has just two patterns — *-bam* and *-ebam* — and you can spot both from a distance in any text.

*Eram* has no *-ba-*, but it has an *-a-* in the same place, so it still sounds similar. The quickest sign that a sentence is about the past is the *-ba-* or *-eba-* insert itself — not the person ending, since *-at* is also used in the group-one present (*portat*, *habitat*). Memorize *eram*, *poteram*, and *ibam* as the three exceptions without that insert.
This one Latin form covers three things English expresses with different helpers: "used to", "was …-ing", and the simple past. Look at the right-hand column.

Translation
What it expresses
rows: I used to live in that house.
Marcus was reading, Iulia was singing.
two actions at the same time

The school was small back then.

blocks.title: Compare with the next form
items: *Cotidie ambulabam.* — "I used to walk every day." A habit, with no clear start or end.
*Heri ambulavi.* — "I walked yesterday." One event, finished. This form arrives in Unit 13.
The quickest test: if you can put "was …-ing", "used to", or "back then" into the English translation, use the imperfect.
In a story, the imperfect sets the scene and the next form moves the plot. Every Latin author alternates between scene and plot like this.

blocks.text: Latin loves marking the sequence of time at the start of a sentence: *primo … deinde … postea … denique*. If you want your story to sound Roman, start your sentences with those words, not with the subject.

blocks.title: Practice telling a story in three sentences
items: *Olim in oppido parvo habitabam.* — I used to live in a small town.
*Cotidie ad scholam ambulabam et cum amicis ridebam.* — Every day I walked to school and laughed with my friends.
*Magister severus erat, sed fabulas bonas narrabat.* — The teacher was strict, but he told good stories.
Copy those three sentences with your own life. Change the place, the habit, the people — the pattern stays.
